claim: Scars are a serious health concern for burn victims and individuals with skin conditions associated with wound healing.
source: Scars are a serious health concern for burn victims and individuals with skin conditions associated with wound healing.
evidence: This is a general statement about the clinical significance of scars, drawing from established medical knowledge.

claim: Neonatal papillary fibroblasts form a transient regenerative cell type that promotes healthy skin regeneration in young skin.
source: Using scRNA-seq to probe unsorted cells from regenerating, scarring, homeostatic, and developing skin, we identified neonatal papillary fibroblasts that form a transient regenerative cell type that promotes healthy skin regeneration in young skin.
evidence: This claim is supported by scRNA-seq data analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: Neonatal papillary fibroblasts are defined by the expression of Lef1.
source: These fibroblasts are defined by the expression of a canonical Wnt transcription factor Lef1
evidence: This is supported by scRNA-seq data and immunostaining validation shown in the manuscript.

claim: Lef1 expression in fibroblasts primes the adult skin macroenvironment to enhance skin repair.
source: we demonstrate that Lef1 expression in fibroblasts primes the adult skin macroenvironment to enhance skin repair, including regeneration of hair follicles with arrector pili muscles in healed wounds.
evidence: This is demonstrated through gain- and loss-of-function genetic mouse models described in the manuscript.

claim: Lef1 expression in fibroblasts enables regeneration of hair follicles with arrector pili muscles in healed wounds.
source: we demonstrate that Lef1 expression in fibroblasts primes the adult skin macroenvironment to enhance skin repair, including regeneration of hair follicles with arrector pili muscles in healed wounds.
evidence: This is supported by immunostaining data showing arrector pili in regenerated hair follicles in Twist-Lef1KI mice.

claim: One of the main characteristics of scars is the absence of hair follicles.
source: One of the main characteristics of scars is the absence of hair follicles, indicating that their regeneration in a wound may be a critical step in achieving scar-less skin repair (Yang and Cotsarelis, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Hair follicle regeneration in a wound may be a critical step in achieving scar-less skin repair.
source: One of the main characteristics of scars is the absence of hair follicles, indicating that their regeneration in a wound may be a critical step in achieving scar-less skin repair (Yang and Cotsarelis, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that scars lack hair follicles, supported by citation.

claim: Human embryonic skin has the capacity to regenerate without scars.
source: Interestingly, human embryonic skin has the capacity to regenerate without scars (Lo et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Neonatal and adult mouse skin has the capacity to regenerate small non-functional hair follicles under specific conditions.
source: Similarly, neonatal and adult mouse skin has the capacity to regenerate small non-functional hair follicles under specific conditions (Figure 1c–d; Ito et al., 2007; Rognoni et al., 2016; Telerman et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and reference to Figure 1c-d showing regenerating hair follicles.

claim: Human and mouse skin are similar in their overall structural complexity.
source: Human and mouse skin are similar in their overall structural complexity, indicating that mouse skin can be a useful model to study skin development and wound repair (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Mouse skin can be a useful model to study skin development and wound repair.
source: Human and mouse skin are similar in their overall structural complexity, indicating that mouse skin can be a useful model to study skin development and wound repair (Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is an inference based on the structural similarity between human and mouse skin, supported by citation.

claim: Murine hair follicle and skin development primarily occurs between embryonic day 12.5 (E12.5) to post-natal day 21 (P21).
source: Murine hair follicle and skin development primarily occurs between embryonic day 12.5 (E12.5) to post-natal day 21 (P21) (Müller-Röver et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Different fibroblast lineages are established during skin development that respond to changes in the environment to support hair follicle and skin development.
source: During this time, different fibroblast lineages are established that respond to the changes in the environment to support hair follicle and skin development (Driskell et al., 2013; Jiang et al., 2018; Rinkevich et al., 2015; Rognoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Fibroblasts that support hair follicle development differentiate from the papillary fibroblast lineage into dermal papilla (DP), dermal sheath (DS), and arrector pili (AP) cells.
source: Fibroblasts that support hair follicle development differentiate from the papillary fibroblast lineage, into dermal papilla (DP), dermal sheath (DS), and arrector pili (AP) cells (Driskell et al., 2013; Plikus et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Reticular fibroblasts cannot differentiate into papillary fibroblast lineages.
source: Reticular fibroblasts, which cannot differentiate into papillary fibroblast lineages, secrete extra-cellular-matrix (ECM) and form adipocytes (Driskell et al., 2013; Schmidt and Horsley, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Reticular fibroblasts secrete extra-cellular-matrix (ECM) and form adipocytes.
source: Reticular fibroblasts, which cannot differentiate into papillary fibroblast lineages, secrete extra-cellular-matrix (ECM) and form adipocytes (Driskell et al., 2013; Schmidt and Horsley, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: By post-natal day 2 (P2) fibroblast heterogeneity is fully established with the presence of defined layers of the dermis.
source: By post-natal day 2 (P2) fibroblast heterogeneity is fully established with the presence of the defined layers of the dermis (Figure 1a; Driskell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation and reference to Figure 1a showing the dermal layers.

claim: Skin maturation occurs after P2 with the formation of the arrector pili and the completion of the first hair follicle cycle.
source: Skin maturation occurs after P2 with the formation of the AP and the completion of the first hair follicle cycle, which results in the loss of a defined papillary fibroblast layer (Figure 1b; Driskell et al., 2013; Rognoni et al., 2016; Salzer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1b.

claim: Skin maturation results in the loss of a defined papillary fibroblast layer.
source: Skin maturation occurs after P2 with the formation of the AP and the completion of the first hair follicle cycle, which results in the loss of a defined papillary fibroblast layer (Figure 1b; Driskell et al., 2013; Rognoni et al., 2016; Salzer et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations and reference to Figure 1b.

claim: Papillary fibroblasts are the primary source of de-novo dermal papilla during skin development.
source: We have previously shown that papillary fibroblasts are the primary source of de-novo dermal papilla during skin development, which are required for hair formation (Driskell et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: De-novo dermal papilla are required for hair formation.
source: We have previously shown that papillary fibroblasts are the primary source of de-novo dermal papilla during skin development, which are required for hair formation (Driskell et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Adult murine skin forms scars due to the lack of a defined papillary layer.
source: Furthermore, it has been suggested that adult murine skin form scars due to the lack of a defined papillary layer (Driskell et al., 2013; Driskell and Watt, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Expanding the papillary fibroblast layer in adult skin might support skin regeneration in adult mice.
source: Consequently, expanding this fibroblast layer in adult skin might support skin regeneration in adult mice.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the observation that adult skin lacks a defined papillary layer.

claim: scRNA-seq studies investigating wound healing have focused on comparing scarring, non-scarring, or regenerating conditions.
source: In addition, scRNA-seq studies investigating wound healing have so far focused on comparing scarring, non-scarring, or regenerating conditions (Guerrero-Juarez et al., 2019; Haensel et al., 2020; Joost et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: scRNA-seq studies have helped identify key markers of the newly discovered skin fascia, including Gpx3, Plac8, and Mest.
source: These studies have helped to identified key markers of the newly discovered skin fascia, including Gpx3, Plac8, and Mest, which recently has been shown to contribute to scar formation (Correa-Gallegos et al., 2019; Grachtchouk et al., 2000; Joost et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Skin fascia markers Gpx3, Plac8, and Mest have been shown to contribute to scar formation.
source: These studies have helped to identified key markers of the newly discovered skin fascia, including Gpx3, Plac8, and Mest, which recently has been shown to contribute to scar formation (Correa-Gallegos et al., 2019; Grachtchouk et al., 2000; Joost et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Transgenic activation of the Shh pathway in alpha-smooth-actin cells in scarring wounds can support small non-functional hair regeneration.
source: These, scRNA-seq studies have revealed that transgenic activation of the Shh pathway in the alpha-smooth-actin cells in scarring wounds, which includes pericytes, blood vessels, and myofibroblasts, can support small non-functional hair regeneration (Lim et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Alpha-smooth-actin cells in scarring wounds include pericytes, blood vessels, and myofibroblasts.
source: These, scRNA-seq studies have revealed that transgenic activation of the Shh pathway in the alpha-smooth-actin cells in scarring wounds, which includes pericytes, blood vessels, and myofibroblasts, can support small non-functional hair regeneration (Lim et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Activation of Shh pathway in dermal fibroblasts is associated with malignant phenotypes.
source: However, activation of Shh pathway in dermal fibroblasts is associated with malignant phenotypes and may perturb development and homeostasis such that it may not be a safe target to support human skin regeneration clinically (Fan et al., 1997; Grachtchouk et al., 2000; Oro et al., 1997; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activation of Shh pathway in dermal fibroblasts may perturb development and homeostasis.
source: However, activation of Shh pathway in dermal fibroblasts is associated with malignant phenotypes and may perturb development and homeostasis such that it may not be a safe target to support human skin regeneration clinically (Fan et al., 1997; Grachtchouk et al., 2000; Oro et al., 1997; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Shh pathway may not be a safe target to support human skin regeneration clinically.
source: However, activation of Shh pathway in dermal fibroblasts is associated with malignant phenotypes and may perturb development and homeostasis such that it may not be a safe target to support human skin regeneration clinically (Fan et al., 1997; Grachtchouk et al., 2000; Oro et al., 1997; Sun et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an inference based on the association of Shh activation with malignant phenotypes, supported by citations.

claim: The Wnt signaling pathway is involved in regulating development, wound healing, disease and cancer.
source: The Wnt signaling pathway is involved in regulating development, wound healing, disease and cancer (Nusse and Clevers, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Studies that activated Wnt and beta-catenin in skin have produced contrasting results in the context of fibroblast biology and hair follicle formation.
source: Studies that activated Wnt and beta-catenin in skin have led to important discoveries for wound healing but have produced contrasting results in the context of fibroblast biology and hair follicle formation (Chen et al., 2012; Enshell-Seijffers et al., 2010; Hamburg-Shields et al., 2015; Lim et al., 2018; Rognoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Beta-catenin cannot activate the expression of Wnt target genes without co-transcription factors.
source: Importantly, beta-catenin alone cannot activate the expression of Wnt target genes without co-transcription factors.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of Wnt signaling mechanisms.

claim: There are four Wnt co-transcription factors: Tcf7 (Tcf1), Lef1, Tcf3 (Tcf7l1), and Tcf4 (Tcf7l2).
source: There are four Wnt co-transcription factors Tcf7 (Tcf1), Lef1, Tcf3 (Tcf7l1), and Tcf4 (Tcf7l2).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge of Wnt signaling components.

claim: Wnt co-transcription factors modulate the functional outcome of Wnt signaling by binding to different target genes.
source: These co-transcription factors modulate the functional outcome of Wnt signaling by binding to different target genes (Adam et al., 2018; Nguyen et al., 2009; Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: It is not known how differential expression of Tcf/Lef can modulate fibroblast activity via Wnt signaling in the context of wound healing and regeneration.
source: In the context of wound healing and regeneration, it is not known how differential expression of Tcf/Lef can modulate fibroblast activity via Wnt signaling.
evidence: This identifies a gap in current knowledge.

claim: Embryonic and neonatal skin have the potential to regenerate hair follicles upon wounding.
source: Since it has been shown that embryonic and neonatal skin have the potential to regenerate hair follicles upon wounding (Hu et al., 2018; Rognoni et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: There are differences between neonatal and adult skin in terms of their cellular and biological properties.
source: We and others have previously shown that there are differences between neonatal and adult skin in terms of their cellular and biological properties (Ge et al., 2020; Rognoni et al., 2016; Salzer et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Differences between neonatal and adult skin influence how skin can repair or if it can regenerate hair follicles in a wound.
source: These differences influence how skin can repair or if it can regenerate hair follicles in a wound.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed differences between neonatal and adult skin.

claim: Neonatal developing skin at P2 can regenerate small hair follicles 7 days after wounding.
source: We showed that neonatal developing skin at P2 (Figure 1a) can regenerate small hair follicles 7 days after wounding (7dpw) (Figure 1c)
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1a and 1c showing the regenerating hair follicles.

claim: Adult homeostatic skin at P21 heals by scarring 7 days post wound.
source: while adult homeostatic skin at P21 (Figure 1b) heals by scarring 7dpw (Figure 1d).
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1b and 1d showing the scar tissue.

claim: A total of 66,407 cells from 12 libraries met the preprocessing threshold for scRNA-seq analysis.
source: A total of 66,407 cells from 12 libraries (n = 3 for each condition) met the preprocessing threshold, showed little batch variation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and were used for downstream analysis.
evidence: This is a direct report of the data processing results.

claim: The scRNA-seq data showed little batch variation.
source: A total of 66,407 cells from 12 libraries (n = 3 for each condition) met the preprocessing threshold, showed little batch variation (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), and were used for downstream analysis.
evidence: This is supported by reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Louvain modulating analysis resulted in 18 distinct clusters.
source: To identify cell clusters, we used Louvain modulating analysis (Joost et al., 2016; Wolf et al., 2018), which resulted in 18 distinct clusters (Figure 1g).
evidence: This is a direct report of the clustering analysis results, supported by Figure 1g.

claim: Keratinocytes represented the largest portion of cell types in the scRNA-seq analysis.
source: Keratinocytes represented the largest portion of cell types in the analysis (blue clusters - 0, 1, 2, 5, 8, 9, 11, 12, 17) (Figure 1h).
evidence: This is supported by the clustering analysis shown in Figure 1h.

claim: Three distinct fibroblast clusters were identified that expressed Twist2, Pdgfra, and En1.
source: We identified three distinct fibroblast clusters (green clusters - 3, 4, 16). These clusters expressed Twist2, Pdgfra, and En1 (Figure 1h).
evidence: This is supported by gene expression analysis shown in Figure 1h.

claim: There was no cluster exclusively defined by over-representation of the regenerating condition.
source: Unexpectedly, there was no cluster exclusively defined by over-representation of the regenerating condition.
evidence: This is based on quantification of cell conditions within clusters.

claim: Cluster 16 consisted of 99.9% of fibroblasts from homeostatic skin.
source: Cluster 16 consisted of 99.9% of fibroblasts from homeostatic skin, while Cluster 3 consisted of 67.8% of developing fibroblasts (Figure 1i).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1i.

claim: Cluster 3 consisted of 67.8% of developing fibroblasts.
source: Cluster 16 consisted of 99.9% of fibroblasts from homeostatic skin, while Cluster 3 consisted of 67.8% of developing fibroblasts (Figure 1i).
evidence: This is supported by quantification shown in Figure 1i.

claim: Fibroblasts play a critical role in regulating hair follicle reformation in wounds by differentiating into de-novo DP.
source: Since fibroblasts are known to play a critical role in regulating hair follicle reformation in wounds by differentiating into de-novo DP (Driskell et al., 2013; Plikus et al., 2017; Rognoni et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Integration analysis of fibroblast clusters revealed 10 distinct clusters.
source: UMAP plotting of the integrated analysis revealed 10 distinct clusters (Figure 1k).
evidence: This is supported by the UMAP plot shown in Figure 1k.

claim: The largest fibroblast cluster (cluster 0) expressed markers of the papillary fibroblast lineage.
source: The largest cluster (cluster 0) expressed markers of the papillary fibroblast lineage (Figure 1e–g).
evidence: This is supported by marker expression analysis.

claim: Four fibroblast clusters distinctly expressed markers of the reticular/hypodermal/fascia layers of the dermis.
source: Four clusters (clusters 1, 2, 3, 4) distinctly expressed markers of the reticular/hypodermal/fascia layers of the dermis (Figure 1k; Figure 1—figure supplement 1a–b; Supplementary file 1; Correa-Gallegos et al., 2019; Joost et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by marker expression analysis and citations.

claim: Three fibroblast clusters expressed markers of the dermal papilla and dermal sheath.
source: Three clusters (clusters 6, 7, 8) expressed markers of the dermal papilla and dermal sheath (Figure 1e–g).
evidence: This is supported by marker expression analysis.

claim: One fibroblast cluster was distinctly represented by Acta2 indicating a myofibroblast subtype.
source: One cluster was distinctly represented by Acta2 indicating a myofibroblast subtype (cluster 9).
evidence: This is based on marker expression analysis.

claim: The myofibroblast sub-cluster (cluster 9) contained 69% of cells from the regenerating condition.
source: The myofibroblast sub-cluster (cluster 9) contained 69% of cells from the regenerating condition
evidence: This is based on quantification of cell conditions within clusters.

claim: A hypodermal fascia cluster (cluster 1) contained 92.2% of cells from the scarring condition.
source: while a hypodermal fascia cluster (cluster 1) contained 92.2% of cells from the scarring condition.
evidence: This is based on quantification of cell conditions within clusters.

claim: Cluster 4, identified by high expression of Cochlin (Coch), contained 80.8% of cells from the homeostasis condition.
source: Cluster 4, identified by the high expression of Cochlin (Coch), an inner ear ECM protein, contained 80.8% of cells from the homeostasis condition
evidence: This is based on quantification of cell conditions within clusters and marker expression.

claim: A DP/DS sub-cluster (cluster 6) contained 95.0% of cells from the homeostasis condition.
source: and a DP/DS sub-clusters (cluster 6) contained 95.0% of cells from the homeostasis condition.
evidence: This is based on quantification of cell conditions within clusters.

claim: The papillary fibroblast cluster (cluster 0) contained 98.1% of cells from the developing skin condition.
source: The papillary fibroblast cluster (cluster 0) contained 98.1% of cells from the developing skin condition.
evidence: This is based on quantification of cell conditions within clusters.

claim: The DP sub-cluster (cluster 7) consisted of 56.5% cells from the developing condition and 37.1% cells from the regenerating condition.
source: The DP sub-cluster (cluster 7) consisted of 56.5% cells from the developing condition and 37.1% cells from the regenerating condition.
evidence: This is based on quantification of cell conditions within clusters.

claim: There is a distinct separation based on condition between fibroblast sub-types neonatal papillary fibroblasts versus reticular/hypodermal/fascia.
source: These results indicate that there is a distinct separation based on condition between fibroblast sub-types neonatal papillary fibroblasts versus reticular/hypodermal/fascia.
evidence: This is an inference based on the quantification of cell conditions within clusters.

claim: Regenerating and scarring conditions were present in similar proportions across multiple fibroblast subtypes.
source: Moreover, regenerating, and scarring conditions were present in similar proportions across multiple fibroblasts subtypes, besides clusters of hypodermal and fascia cells that were mainly composed of the scarring condition.
evidence: This is based on quantification of cell conditions within clusters.

claim: Both wounding conditions shared similar cellular and molecular signatures that may be driven by the wound healing process.
source: This suggested that both wounding conditions shared similar cellular and molecular signatures that may be driven by the wound healing process.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity in cell type proportions between regenerating and scarring conditions.

claim: Developing fibroblasts migrate into wounds and support the reformation of hair follicles.
source: Developing fibroblasts migrate into wounds and support the reformation of hair follicles (Driskell et al., 2013; Rognoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: DP and DS do not migrate into wounds to support hair follicle reformation in homeostatic skin.
source: In homeostatic skin DP and DS are critical for hair follicle growth and cycling. However, they do not migrate into wounds to support hair follicle reformation (Johnston et al., 2013; Kaushal et al., 2015; Abbasi et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Myofibroblasts are a major contributor to scar formation.
source: Myofibroblasts are a major contributor to scar formation but may not normally differentiate into dermal papilla during hair follicle regeneration (Lim et al., 2018; Plikus et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Myofibroblasts may not normally differentiate into dermal papilla during hair follicle regeneration.
source: Myofibroblasts are a major contributor to scar formation but may not normally differentiate into dermal papilla during hair follicle regeneration (Lim et al., 2018; Plikus et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Reticular and fascia fibroblasts contribute to scar formation but do not differentiate into dermal papilla.
source: Furthermore, reticular and fascia fibroblasts contribute to scar formation but do not differentiate into dermal papilla (Correa-Gallegos et al., 2019; Driskell et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The developing fibroblasts are unique and might harbor the potential to support hair follicle regeneration in wounds.
source: We conclude that the developing fibroblasts are unique and might harbor the potential to support hair follicle regeneration in wounds.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the analysis of fibroblast subtypes and their properties.

claim: Previously identified fibroblast heterogeneity and lineages could be identified in the scRNA-seq analysis of developing skin.
source: Overall, we concluded that the previously identified fibroblasts heterogeneity and the lineages could be identified in the scRNA-seq analysis of developing skin, with the additional subclusters of papillary fibroblasts (Figure 2e; Driskell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is based on comparison of scRNA-seq data with previously published lineage markers.

claim: Novel heterogeneity within papillary fibroblast clusters was found, with Lef1 and Dkk1 expressions marking distinct papillary fibroblast clusters.
source: Interestingly, we also found novel heterogeneity within papillary fibroblast clusters. Besides the Dpp4+ clusters, Lef1 and Dkk1 expressions marked distinct papillary fibroblast clusters (Figure 2i, Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on gene expression analysis in scRNA-seq data.

claim: RNA velocity analysis predicts that the dermal papilla is a differentiation endpoint.
source: Velocity analysis predicts that the dermal papilla is a differentiation endpoint, while papillary fibroblasts converge into the Dpp4 subcluster.
evidence: This is based on RNA velocity computational analysis.

claim: RNA velocity analysis predicts that papillary fibroblasts converge into the Dpp4 subcluster.
source: Velocity analysis predicts that the dermal papilla is a differentiation endpoint, while papillary fibroblasts converge into the Dpp4 subcluster.
evidence: This is based on RNA velocity computational analysis.

claim: The predicted differentiation trajectory of reticular fibroblasts suggests that they differentiate into arrector pili and also converge into the Dpp4 papillary subcluster.
source: Interestingly, the predicted differentiation trajectory of reticular fibroblasts suggests that they differentiate into arrector pili and also converge into the Dpp4 papillary subcluster.
evidence: This is based on RNA velocity computational analysis.

claim: The RNA velocity prediction that reticular fibroblasts differentiate into papillary fibroblasts contradicts previous in vivo lineage-tracing studies.
source: This contradicts previous in vivo lineage-tracing studies of the Dlk1+ fibroblast populations but agrees with ex vivo studies that tested the differentiation potential of Dpp4-/Dlk1+/Ly6a- fibroblast populations in chamber grafting and hydrogel assays (Driskell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison between computational predictions and previous experimental studies.

claim: The RNA velocity prediction that reticular fibroblasts differentiate into papillary fibroblasts agrees with ex vivo studies testing differentiation potential in chamber grafting and hydrogel assays.
source: This contradicts previous in vivo lineage-tracing studies of the Dlk1+ fibroblast populations but agrees with ex vivo studies that tested the differentiation potential of Dpp4-/Dlk1+/Ly6a- fibroblast populations in chamber grafting and hydrogel assays (Driskell et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a comparison between computational predictions and previous experimental studies.

claim: Hypodermal and fascia fibroblast clusters were predicted to maintain the lower lineage.
source: Hypodermal and fascia fibroblast clusters were predicted to maintain the lower lineage (Figure 2f).
evidence: This is based on RNA velocity analysis shown in Figure 2f.

claim: The most highly represented pathways in RNA velocity driver genes included Integrin signaling, Wnt signaling, Cadherin signaling and TGFb signaling pathways.
source: We performed PANTHER pathway classification on this list genes and found that the most highly represented pathways included Integrin signaling, Wnt signaling, Cadherin signaling and TGFb signaling pathways (Figure 2h; Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This is based on pathway analysis of RNA velocity driver genes.

claim: Lef1 was found in the Papillary Dkk1 fibroblasts and the Dividing Papillary subclusters as a velocity driver gene.
source: Interestingly, Lef1 was found in the Papillary Dkk1 fibroblasts and the Dividing Papillary subclusters (Figure 2i).
evidence: This is based on analysis of top velocity driver genes for each cluster.

claim: The expression of Lef1 may drive RNA velocity toward papillary fibroblast and dermal papilla.
source: This suggests that the expression of Lef1 may drive RNA velocity toward papillary fibroblast and dermal papilla.
evidence: This is an inference based on the identification of Lef1 as a velocity driver gene.

claim: Phase contrast analysis predicts that Lef1 and Wnt5a velocity increases towards the papillary fibroblast and dermal papilla clusters.
source: Phase contrast analysis predicts that Lef1 and Wnt5a velocity increases towards to the papillary fibroblast and dermal papilla clusters (Figure 2j–k).
evidence: This is based on phase contrast analysis of Wnt signaling genes.

claim: Immunostaining confirmed the population of neonatal papillary fibroblasts expressing Lef1 is found only in developing skin and not in juvenile homeostatic skin.
source: Our results confirmed the population of neonatal papillary fibroblasts that is found only in developing skin (Figure 2j, red arrows) and not in juvenile homeostatic skin (Figure 2k, white arrows).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining validation shown in Figure 2j-k.

claim: Co-staining with Dpp4 confirmed that Lef1 marked a subset of neonatal papillary fibroblasts.
source: Co-staining with Dpp4 confirmed that Lef1 marked a subset of neonatal papillary fibroblasts (Figure 2l) that was also not found in juvenile skin (Figure 2m).
evidence: This is based on co-immunostaining shown in Figure 2l-m.

claim: The transient expression of Lef1 in neonatal papillary fibroblast correlates with the ability of neonatal developing skin to regenerate hair follicles in wounds.
source: The transient expression of Lef1 in neonatal papillary fibroblast correlates with the ability of neonatal developing skin to regenerate hair follicles in wounds (Rognoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a correlation based on the temporal expression pattern of Lef1 and regenerative capacity, supported by citation.

claim: Velocity analysis predicts that Lef1 drives developing fibroblast velocity to papillary fibroblast and DP.
source: In addition, velocity analysis predicts that Lef1 drives developing fibroblast velocity to papillary fibroblast and DP.
evidence: This is based on RNA velocity analysis.

claim: Subset analysis of regenerating and scarring fibroblasts did not identify fibroblasts defined by Lef1 expression.
source: Importantly, subset analysis of regenerating and scarring fibroblasts did not identify fibroblasts defined by Lef1 expression, indicating that this transient population is unique to developing skin (Figure 2—figure supplement 2a–f; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on comparative analysis of fibroblast populations across conditions.

claim: Lef1 expression in fibroblasts marks the ability of developing skin to regenerate hair follicles during the wound healing process.
source: We hypothesize that Lef1 expression in fibroblasts marks the ability of developing skin to regenerate hair follicles during the wound healing process.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the correlation between Lef1 expression and regenerative capacity.

claim: Lef1 in fibroblasts is required to support neonatal regeneration.
source: To test if Lef1 in fibroblasts is required to support neonatal regeneration, we produced a tissue-specific knockout model.
evidence: This is tested through a loss-of-function genetic experiment.

claim: Twist-Lef1cKO mice were viable and fertile with small shifts in hair follicle phenotypes that resulted in less dense fur.
source: Twist-Lef1cKO mice were viable and fertile with small shifts in hair follicle phenotypes that resulted in less dense fur (Fine et al., 2020).
evidence: This is an observation of the phenotype of the knockout mice, supported by citation.

claim: Dermal Lef1 ablation from the papillary fibroblast at P2 and from adult DP was confirmed by immunostaining.
source: We confirmed dermal Lef1 ablation from the papillary fibroblast at P2 and from adult DP by immunostaining (Figure 3b–e).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining validation shown in Figure 3b-e.

claim: Lef1 was expressed in the de-novo DP and regenerating hair follicle buds of wild-type mice at P2 7dpw.
source: Our analyses revealed that Lef1 was expressed in the de-novo DP and regenerating hair follicle buds of wild-type mice (Figure 3g,i)
evidence: This is based on immunostaining analysis shown in Figure 3g,i.

claim: Wounded Twist-Lef1cKO mice lacked regeneration at P2 7dpw.
source: but that wounded Twist-Lef1cKO mice lacked regeneration (Figure 3h,j,k).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining and quantification shown in Figure 3h,j,k.

claim: Lef1 expression in neonatal fibroblasts is required for neonatal hair follicle regeneration in wounds.
source: We conclude that Lef1 expression in neonatal fibroblasts is required for neonatal hair follicle regeneration in wounds.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the loss-of-function experiment showing lack of regeneration in Twist-Lef1cKO mice.

claim: Constitutively active Lef1 expression in dermal fibroblasts will prime skin to support regeneration.
source: We hypothesize that constitutively active Lef1 expression in dermal fibroblasts will prime skin to support regeneration.
evidence: This is a hypothesis to be tested with gain-of-function experiments.

claim: Lef1 was expressed in all dermal fibroblast compartments in Twist-Lef1KI mice during development and in adult homeostatic skin conditions.
source: We verified that Lef1 was expressed in all dermal fibroblast compartments in Twist-Lef1KI mice during development and in adult homeostatic skin conditions (Figure 4b–e).
evidence: This is based on immunostaining validation shown in Figure 4b-e.

claim: The only phenotype detected in Twist-Lef1KI mice was the early entry of the hair follicle cycling into anagen at P21.
source: Importantly, the only phenotype detected was the early entry of the hair follicle cycling into anagen at P21 in Twist-Lef1KI mice (Figure 2d–e).
evidence: This is based on observation of hair follicle cycling in Twist-Lef1KI mice.

claim: Twist-Lef1KI mice have similar life spans as wild type mice without any adverse effects.
source: In addition, Twist-Lef1KI mice have similar life spans as wild type mice without any adverse effects (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on longitudinal observation of the mice shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Induced expression of Lef1 in fibroblasts does not negatively affect the development and homeostasis of murine skin.
source: Our results reveal that induced expression of Lef1 in fibroblasts does not negatively affect the development and homeostasis of murine skin.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observation that Twist-Lef1KI mice are viable with minimal phenotypic changes.

claim: There were five times more regenerating hair follicles on average in Twist-Lef1KI wound beds compared to wild type wounds.
source: There were five times more regenerating hair follicles on average in Twist-Lef1KI wound beds compared to wild type wounds (Figure 4j–k).
evidence: This is based on quantification of regenerating hair follicles shown in Figure 4j-k.

claim: The hair follicles regenerating in the Twist-Lef1KI wound beds contained arrector pili.
source: Strikingly, the hair follicles regenerating in the Twist-Lef1KI wound beds contained arrector pili (Figure 4i)
evidence: This is based on immunostaining for arrector pili marker shown in Figure 4i.

claim: Hair follicles regenerating in Twist-Lef1KI wound beds were larger than hair follicles found in wild-type wounds.
source: and were larger than hair follicles found in wild-type wounds.
evidence: This is based on morphological comparison of regenerated hair follicles.

claim: Lef1 expression in the dermis of the skin leads to enhanced regeneration.
source: We conclude that Lef1 expression in the dermis of the skin leads to enhances regeneration.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the gain-of-function experiment showing enhanced regeneration in Twist-Lef1KI mice.

claim: Wound healing studies utilize a standardized approach to account for the hair follicle cycle, which influences the wound healing process.
source: Wound healing studies utilize a standardized approach to account for the hair follicle cycle, which influences the wound healing process (Ansell et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The bulk of wound healing and regeneration studies are performed at 3 weeks of age (~P21) or at 7–8 weeks of age (~P57).
source: Consequently, the bulk of wound healing and regeneration studies are performed at 3 weeks of age (~P21) or at 7–8 weeks of age (~P57) (Gay et al., 2013; Guerrero-Juarez et al., 2019; Ito et al., 2007; Lim et al., 2018; Plikus et al., 2017; Plikus et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: A standard size wound of roughly 8 mm in diameter or smaller is used in wound healing studies, which heal by scarring.
source: In addition, a standard size wound of roughly 8 mm in diameter or smaller is used, which heal by scarring (Driskell et al., 2013; Lim et al., 2018; Rognoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Scars formed in wounds performed at P24 in both WT and Twist-Lef1KI mice.
source: Scars formed in wounds performed at P24 in both WT and Twist-Lef1KI mice (Figure 5b–c,l).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis shown in Figure 5b-c,l.

claim: Hair follicle regeneration with arrector pili occurred in wounds performed at P40 and P90 in Twist-Lef1KI mice.
source: However, hair follicle regeneration with arrector pili occurred in wounds performed at P40 and P90 in Twist-Lef1KI mice (Figure 5d–k,l; Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on histological analysis and immunostaining shown in Figure 5d-k,l and supplementary figures.

claim: Lef1 expression in the dermis induces skin to support hair follicle regeneration in wounds with variation depending on the timepoints and hair follicle cycle.
source: We conclude that Lef1 expression in the dermis induces skin to support hair follicle regeneration in wounds with variation depends on the timepoints and hair follicle cycle.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the differential regeneration outcomes at different time points.

claim: The size of a wound can dictate the potential of skin to regenerate instead of scar.
source: Our wound healing studies mirror previous work suggesting that the size of a wound can dictate the potential of skin to regenerate instead of scar (Ito et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature and the authors' own observations.

claim: 8 mm circular wounds re-epithelialize 7 days post wound in a macro-environment with high levels of Lef1 inhibitors.
source: 8 mm circular wounds re-epithelialize 7 dpw (Driskell et al., 2013) in a macro-environment with high levels of Lef1 inhibitors, which are not inductive to hair follicle formation (Figure 5l).
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene expression during hair follicle cycling shown in Figure 5l, supported by citation.

claim: Large 1.2 cm2 wounds re-epithelialize during the time point of the hair cycle that has high activators and low inhibitors.
source: In contrast, large 1.2 cm2 wounds re-epithelialize during the time point of the hair cycle that has high activators and low inhibitors (Figure 5l).
evidence: This is based on analysis of gene expression during hair follicle cycling shown in Figure 5l.

claim: The size of a wound dictates the time point when wound closure occurs which is associated with inhibitor or inductive regenerative signals.
source: We conclude that the size of a wound dictates the time point when wound closure occurs which is associated with inhibitor or inductive regenerative signals.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the correlation between wound size, closure timing, and gene expression patterns.

claim: Embryonic and neonatal skin has the potential to heal in a scar-less manner.
source: It is well established that embryonic and neonatal skin has the potential to heal in a scar-less manner (Walmsley et al., 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The cell types and signals that can transfer the regenerative ability of embryonic/neonatal skin to adult skin have not been identified prior to this study.
source: However, the cell types and signals that can transfer this ability to adult skin have not been identified.
evidence: This identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Developing papillary fibroblasts are a transient cell population defined by Lef1 expression.
source: In this study, we identify developing papillary fibroblasts as a transient cell population that is defined by Lef1 expression.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Inducing Lef1 expression in the adult dermis will prime skin to support enhanced hair follicle regeneration.
source: Inducing Lef1 expression in the adult dermis will prime skin to support enhanced hair follicle regeneration.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding from the gain-of-function experiments.

claim: Ectopic Lef1 expression in the dermis did not result in any adverse phenotypes during development.
source: Interestingly, ectopic Lef1 expression in the dermis did not result in any adverse phenotypes during development (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is based on observation of Twist-Lef1KI mice during development.

claim: Comparisons of regenerating and scarring wounds reveal their similarities more than their differences.
source: Unexpectedly, we discovered a neonatal papillary fibroblast population that is defined by Lef1 expression in developing skin instead of in regenerating conditions. Importantly, our comparative analysis of regenerating and scarring wounds reveals their similarities (Figure 1i, Figure 2—figure supplement 2) more than their differences
evidence: This is based on comparative scRNA-seq analysis.

claim: The wound environment is a powerful driving force for gene expression even with a heterogeneous population of cells.
source: suggesting that the wound environment is a powerful driving force for gene expression even with a heterogeneous population of cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the similarity between regenerating and scarring conditions.

claim: The basic mechanisms occurring during development and maintenance of neonatal tissue may hold the keys to transforming adult tissue to regenerate instead of scarring.
source: Consequently, the basic mechanisms occurring during development and maintenance of neonatal tissue may hold the keys to transforming adult tissue to regenerate instead of scarring.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the finding that developing fibroblasts, not wound-induced cells, drive regeneration.

claim: Studies involving the activation of Wnt and beta-catenin pathways in skin have produced contrasting results in the context of fibroblast biology and hair follicle formation.
source: Studies involving the activation of the Wnt and beta-catenin pathways in skin have led to important discoveries in wound healing research, but have produced contrasting results in the context of fibroblast biology and hair follicle formation (Chen et al., 2012; Hamburg-Shields et al., 2015; Ito et al., 2007; Lim et al., 2018; Mastrogiannaki et al., 2016; Rognoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The activation of beta-catenin in fibroblasts during wound healing has been shown to inhibit hair follicle reformation in scars.
source: The activation of beta-catenin in fibroblasts during wound healing has been shown to inhibit hair follicle reformation in scars (Lim et al., 2018; Rognoni et al., 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Deactivating Wnt signaling inhibited hair reformation.
source: while deactivating Wnt signaling inhibited hair reformation (Myung et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: Persistent Wnt activity in the dermis has been shown to drive WIHN toward fibrotic wound healing.
source: Moreover, persistent Wnt activity in the dermis has been recently shown to drive WIHN toward fibrotic wound healing (Gay et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: The activation of beta-catenin during development increases hair formation and size.
source: In contrast, the activation of beta-catenin during development increases hair formation and size (Chen et al., 2012; Enshell-Seijffers et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The presence of different fibroblast lineages in development or wounds, which express different Lef/Tcf factors, may explain conflicting results of Wnt/beta-catenin activation.
source: One explanation for these conflicting results is the presence of different fibroblast lineages present in either development or wounds, which express different Lef/Tcf factors to direct a Wnt/beta-catenin-specific response (Driskell et al., 2013; Philippeos et al., 2018; Rognoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an explanation proposed by the authors, supported by citations.

claim: Lef1 is expressed in embryonic and neonatal papillary fibroblasts, which is lost in adult fibroblasts.
source: We and others have shown that Lef1 is expressed in embryonic and neonatal papillary fibroblasts, which is lost in adult fibroblasts (Driskell et al., 2013; Mastrogiannaki et al., 2016; Philippeos et al., 2018; Rognoni et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature including the authors' own work.

claim: Lef1 is a key transcription factor in developing fibroblasts that supports hair follicle formation in adult wounds.
source: Here, we demonstrate that Lef1 is a key transcription factor in developing fibroblasts that supports hair follicle formation in adult wounds.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding of the study.

claim: Lef1 expression in the dermis of the skin primes a response to support hair follicle neogenesis and arrector pili reformation in the wound.
source: Our data indicates that Lef1 expression in the dermis of the skin primes a response to support hair follicle neogenesis and arrector pili reformation in the wound.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the gain-of-function experiments.

claim: Inducing Lef1 expression in cultured human dermal papilla cells enhances hair follicle formation in vitro.
source: Our results align with studies that induced Lef1 expression in cultured human dermal papilla cells to enhance hair follicle formation in vitro (Abaci et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: At the age of 50+, the quality of the papillary dermis gradually deteriorates in humans.
source: In humans, at the age of 50+, the quality of the papillary dermis gradually deteriorates, which correlates with the aging skin decreased wound healing abilities (Haydont et al., 2019; Marcos-Garcés et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The deterioration of the papillary dermis correlates with aging skin's decreased wound healing abilities.
source: In humans, at the age of 50+, the quality of the papillary dermis gradually deteriorates, which correlates with the aging skin decreased wound healing abilities (Haydont et al., 2019; Marcos-Garcés et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Activating the papillary region to retain its identity by expression of Lef1 has the potential to enhance wound healing in humans.
source: Our data suggests that activating the papillary region to retain its identity by expression of Lef1 has the potential to enhance wound healing in humans.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from mouse data to potential human applications.
